opus-5.5.text:
I think most people still picture AI as automation: take something a human already does, like reading a document or answering a support ticket, and do it faster and cheaper. That's valuable, but it's fundamentally bounded by human performance. You're copying what we already know how to do.

What gets me excited is when the system discovers something we didn't know. I saw this firsthand working on industrial control, cooling large data centers. These facilities are run by very experienced engineers who've spent decades building intuitions and rules of thumb. When we let a reinforcement learning agent learn from the system itself, it didn't just match those operators. It found strategies that seemed counterintuitive at first. It would do things like run more equipment at lower load, or anticipate changes in a way no rulebook prescribed, and the result was meaningfully more efficient. The operators' first reaction was often, "That's wrong." Then they'd look at the data and realize it had found something real about the physics of their own plant.

That's what I mean by creativity. It isn't writing a poem. It's searching a space of possibilities far bigger than any person can hold in their head, and coming back with solutions that are genuinely new and verifiably better. It's the AlphaGo move 37 moment, but applied to the physical world: energy, manufacturing, water, pharmaceuticals.

The reason I think that's the real promise is the scale of the upside. If AI only imitates us, the ceiling is human-level productivity at lower cost. If AI can discover, the ceiling is wherever the physics actually is, and in most industrial systems we're nowhere near it. There's enormous efficiency still on the table, which matters a lot for things like energy use and climate.

There's an important caveat. In the physical world, creativity has to be trustworthy. You can't let an agent experiment freely on a power plant. So a lot of the hard work is building systems that can be creative within safe constraints, explain their reasoning well enough that operators trust them, and keep learning as conditions change. When you get that right, the AI stops being a tool that does what you tell it and becomes a collaborator that shows you what's possible.

r001.rationale: The response says automation is valuable but bounded by copying human performance, while discovery offers a greater potential.

r002.rationale: It defines creativity as discovering what people did not know and finding genuinely new, verifiably better solutions.

r003.rationale: The agent reveals counterintuitive strategies to experienced operators, but the response does not say those experts helped design the agent.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, when people talk about AI they usually jump straight to efficiency, and I get that, because that's where I started. My first big project at Google was using machine learning to cut cooling energy in our data centers. We took the same approach we'd used to learn Atari games and pointed it at a very physical problem, and the system found ways to run the plant that none of our engineers would have tried. It was lowering the water temperature at times we would have considered counterintuitive, running more chillers at partial load instead of fewer at full load. It was a forty percent reduction in cooling energy, which was great, but the thing that stuck with me wasn't the number. It was that the system had done something genuinely novel. It had explored a space we had already assumed we understood.

That's why I think creativity is the real promise. Efficiency is about doing what we already know how to do, faster or cheaper. Creativity is about expanding the set of things we know how to do at all. And the hard problems we actually care about, in energy, in industrial systems, in climate, aren't bottlenecked on execution. They're bottlenecked on ideas. A good engineer at a power plant or a steel mill has decades of intuition, but they've only ever operated inside the range of conditions they've personally seen. An AI system can explore a far wider range, including the parts that feel uncomfortable or wrong to a human, and that's often exactly where the breakthroughs are hiding.

What I saw with AlphaGo was the same thing. Move 37 wasn't a faster version of what a human would do. It was a move no human would have made, and it turned out to be beautiful. I think we're going to see Move 37 moments in physical infrastructure, and that's what gets me out of bed. Not AI as a cost-cutting tool, but AI as a collaborator that helps us see possibilities we were blind to.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts efficiency with creativity and says AI’s promise is expanding what we know how to do, rather than merely cutting costs or doing familiar tasks faster.

r002.rationale: It defines creativity as expanding the set of things we know how to do and describes the system finding genuinely novel approaches in a space engineers thought they understood.

r003.rationale: The response says the system found nonobvious ways to run a data center, but does not clearly state that the narrator was an expert who helped design the agent and received those insights.

astra-6.text:
I think the real promise of AI is that it can help us discover things we wouldn’t have thought of ourselves. Automating something we already know how to do is valuable. But there’s a much bigger opportunity in expanding the set of ideas we can explore.

When you’re working on a hard problem, you bring experience and intuition, but you also bring assumptions. You have a sense of what should work, and that can limit what you try. An AI system can explore possibilities outside those habits and come back with something surprising. Then you have to ask: Does this actually work? What did it find that we missed?

That’s the kind of creativity that excites me. It doesn’t have to look like human creativity to be useful. If it helps us find a better solution, or understand something we couldn’t understand before, it expands what we’re capable of doing.

r001.rationale: The response says automation is valuable but that AI offers a much bigger opportunity by expanding the ideas and possibilities we can explore.

r002.rationale: It describes discovering ideas or insights people had not considered, but does not say AI acquires knowledge that did not previously exist.

r003.rationale: It says AI can surface surprising possibilities, but does not describe revealing unknown insights about a system to the expert who designed the agent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the real promise of AI is that it can help us discover things we wouldn’t have thought of ourselves. Automating something we already know how to do is valuable, but finding a solution that wasn’t on our radar—that expands what we’re capable of.

And I mean creativity in a broad sense. It could be a new scientific hypothesis, a different engineering design, or an unexpected way to solve a practical problem. The exciting part is the partnership: we bring the goals, the context, and the judgment, and AI helps us explore a much wider space of possibilities. That gives us a chance to move beyond making existing processes more efficient and actually create something new.

r001.rationale: It says automation of known tasks is valuable but limited, while AI can help find solutions beyond our radar and create something new.

r002.rationale: It describes discovering ideas and solutions people had not considered, but does not clearly define creativity as acquiring previously nonexistent knowledge.

r003.rationale: It describes AI helping people explore possibilities, but not an AI agent revealing system insights to the expert who designed it.
